steps.title: Match each adverb with its meaning.
Two moments when something went wrong.
steps.sub: In each one, a long action is interrupted by a short one.

items.text: I was having lunch with a friend when a man came over.
We were just beginning to land when the plane took off again.

steps.title: Look at the two sentences again.
steps.sub: I was having lunch when a man came over.
options: Having lunch — the long action, in the Past Continuous.
The man coming over — the short action, in the Past Simple.
Neither of them: they started at exactly the same moment.
steps.answer: Having lunch — the long action, in the Past Continuous.
steps.why: The Past Continuous is the long action already in progress; the Past Simple interrupts it.

steps.title: while and when
steps.html:
The long action (in progress)The short action (interrupts)
I was having lunchwhen a man came over.
While we were putting our boots on,the weather changed.
She was sitting opposite mewhen the straw jumped out of my mouth.
What were you doingwhen you got home?
They weren’t listeningwhen he asked for directions.

Past Continuous = was / were + -ing. Use it for the longer action that was already happening.

Past Simple = the shorter action that came into the middle of it.

While is normally followed by the long action; when is normally followed by the short one.

Two long actions at the same time both take the Past Continuous: The sun was shining and I was looking out of the window.

You will put these two tenses together in a whole story in the next lesson.

steps.title: Now listen to a psychologist talking about lifts.
steps.prompt: What happens when a second person enters the lift?
options: The two people stand in opposite corners.
They start a conversation about the weather.
They both turn and look at the door.
steps.answer: The two people stand in opposite corners.

steps.title: Now listen to a psychologist talking about lifts.
steps.prompt: What shape do four people make?
options: A square, one person in each corner.
A triangle, with the fourth person outside.
A line of four along one wall.
steps.answer: A square, one person in each corner.

steps.title: Now listen to a psychologist talking about lifts.
steps.prompt: Where does a fifth person probably stand?
steps.answer: In the middle.

steps.title: Listen to part 2: what people do.
steps.prompt: What does everybody do as soon as they enter a lift?
steps.answer: They turn around.

steps.title: Listen to part 2: what people do.
steps.prompt: What do people never do in a lift?
options: Make eye contact with the others.
Look down at the floor of the lift.
Look at the buttons on the wall.
steps.answer: Make eye contact with the others.

steps.title: Listen to part 2: what people do.
steps.prompt: Why do people behave like this, according to the psychologist?
options: Small spaces make us anxious, so we try not to make others nervous.
It is a written rule in most buildings, and people simply follow it.
Most people are in a hurry and have no time to talk to a stranger.
steps.answer: Small spaces make us anxious, so we try not to make others nervous.

steps.title: Listen again. True or False?
steps.prompt: Everybody says hello politely in a lift.
steps.answer: False

steps.title: Listen again. True or False?
steps.prompt: Two people who come in together often start speaking more quietly.
steps.answer: True
